abstract: Plants are continuously challenged by biotic and abiotic stresses that compromise growth, productivity, and stress resilience. Although bulk omics approaches have identified numerous stress-responsive pathways, they obscure the cellular heterogeneity and spatial organization that underlie stress perception, signal transmission, and response execution. Single-cell and spatial omics now enable plant stress responses to be resolved at the levels of cell type, cell state, and spatial location. In this review, we synthesize recent applications of single-cell RNA sequencing, single-nucleus RNA sequencing, single-cell chromatin accessibility profiling, spatial transcriptomics, and emerging single-cell proteomics in plant stress biology. We systematically compare biotic and abiotic stresses in terms of spatial response patterns, cellular division of labor, cell-state transitions, and gene regulatory networks. Biotic stress typically generates localized, infection-centered immune landscapes characterized by sentinel-cell activation, vascular defense hubs, and receptor-triggered transcriptional cascades. In contrast, abiotic stress more commonly involves organ-scale homeostatic adjustment, developmental plasticity, and sustained growth-tolerance trade-offs. Despite these distinctions, both stress classes share core regulatory modules, including reactive oxygen species, hormone signaling, transcription factor networks, and vascular long-distance communication. We further discuss technical challenges related to protoplast and nuclei preparation, cell-type annotation, spatial resolution, and multimodal data integration. By linking stress-responsive genes to the specific cell types, states, and spatial domains in which they function, single-cell approaches provide a mechanistic framework for precision engineering and breeding of stress-resilient crops.
